Full text

Abstract

We report no conflicts of interest. We thank Xinlei Wang, Lara Gawrilowa and Matsik Frumosu for their help in the screening and coding work, and Maien Sachisthal for reviewing an earlier draft. We are grateful to librarian Janneke Staak for support in developing the search strings.

[div-01]

Human behavior is a major driver of environmental problems, including biodiversity loss and climate change. A shift in human behavior is needed to prevent the worst potential outcomes, and encouraging more pro-environmental behavior is key to addressing climate change (Whitmarsh et al., 2021). There is growing interest in leveraging emotions to motivate pro-environmental behaviors (Brosch, 2025; Carmi et al., 2015; Fernández-Ferrín et al., 2024; Mishra et al., 2024; Yan et al., 2024). Although early research primarily focused on negative emotions like guilt and fear, emerging evidence suggests that positive emotions may also facilitate pro-environmental intentions and behaviors (e.g., Strömbäck et al., 2025; Zhou, Brick, et al., 2026). If this positive association between positive emotions and behaviors is robust, it could potentially reflect a self-perpetuating positive feedback loop, in which people feel better when acting green and then continue with more green actions and subsequently experience positive feelings (Brosch, 2021; Brosch & Steg, 2021; Schneider & van der Linden, 2023). This possibility has spurred research across several disciplines, including psychology, economics, and marketing. However, the findings have not yet been systematically synthesized, preventing a comprehensive understanding of whether positive emotions are consistently related to pro-environmental behavior. Here, we provide a systematic review and meta-analysis to test the robustness of the associations between positive emotions and pro-environmental intentions and behaviors.

Emotions and Pro-Environmental Behaviors

Most current efforts to address climate change in behavioral science focus on understanding and changing cognitive factors related to behavior change, such as psychological distance and environmental values (Kollmann et al., 2026; Langlais et al., 2026). There is strong evidence linking these factors to self-reported pro-environmental behaviors, including sustainable consumption and conservation behaviors (Aktan & Kethüda, 2024; Aprile & Fiorillo, 2017; Chen et al., 2022). However, an exclusive focus on cognition may not fully explain why people do or do not engage in pro-environmental behaviors (Kollmuss & Agyeman, 2002). Interest is therefore broadening towards a wider range of socio-emotional factors like social identity and conformity (Farrow et al., 2017; Prati et al., 2017; Thye, 2025). In particular, emotions are emerging as a new domain of study in the context of pro-environmental behaviors (Brosch, 2021; Brosch & Sauter, 2023; Schneider et al., 2021). This work is showing considerable promise, with a growing body of research highlighting the explanatory and predictive value of emotions in understanding human responses to current climate and ecological crises.

Climate change is a highly emotional issue. People often experience intense negative emotions, such as anxiety and worry, in relation to changes in the climate and environment.

Previous research has primarily focused on understanding how negative emotions can motivate pro-environmental behaviors (Kovács et al., 2024). This work has found that people who feel more negative emotions in relation to climate change are more likely to take action (Ogunbode et al., 2022; Schwarz et al., 2026). However, negative feelings can be overwhelming and potentially result in negative consequences, including reduced climate action (Davidson & Kecinski, 2022) and poor subjective wellbeing (Lutz et al., 2023; Ogunbode et al., 2022; Rana et al., 2026). Complementing research into negative emotions, emerging work suggests a promising role for positive emotions in shaping pro-environmental intention and behaviors. Indeed, a recent meta-analysis suggests that positive emotions, such as hope, are associated with increased climate action (Geiger et al., 2023; Schwarz et al., 2026). This work has focused on emotions relating to the climate, rather than emotions anticipated before or experienced after engaging in climate-relevant behaviors. However, evidence suggests that behavior-related emotional responses can also influence subsequent pro-environmental behaviors (Bissing-Olson et al., 2016). This distinction is important as behavior-related emotional responses may provide immediate feedback that can either reinforce or discourage future engagement.

Warm Glow and Pro-Environmental Intentions and Behaviors

Warm glow is a behavior-related emotional response that captures a specific type of positive emotional experience. It is typically defined as the intrinsic satisfaction and pleasure people can experience from acting pro-socially (Andreoni, 1990; Cahyasita et al., 2021; Taufik et al., 2015). Warm glow has been widely studied in the context of prosocial behaviors (Bianchi et al., 2023; Ferguson et al., 2012). Recent work suggests that people also experience warm glow after engaging in pro-environmental behaviors (Taufik et al., 2015; Zhou, Brick, et al., 2026). Pro-environmental behaviors can be seen as a form of prosocial behavior, as both involve acting for the benefit of others. However, pro-environmental behaviors often benefit a broader set of targets, including animals, ecosystems and future generations, whereas prosocial behaviors usually benefit other individuals or specific groups of people. Despite the extensive body of research in the context of prosocial behaviors, it remains unclear whether warm glow is associated with pro-environmental behavior.

Warm glow has been defined in conceptually distinct ways. Some studies have emphasized moral self-appraisal related to self-identity (e.g., feeling like a good or environmentally responsible person; Chen et al., 2025; Mahasuweerachai & Suttikun, 2022; Venhoeven et al., 2016), while other studies highlight feelings of satisfaction from proenvironmental behaviors (Rahnama Haratbar et al., 2024; Wang et al., 2023). Here, we define warm glow as immediate, self-related positive feelings (e.g., feeling good, proud and satisfied) that people can experience from acting pro-environmentally when such actions align with their personal values (Chen et al., 2025; Venhoeven et al., 2016).

This definition distinguishes warm glow from emotional responses to climate change, which are typically other-focused. For example, a person may feel worried about the impacts of climate change or angry about others' inaction. Our definition emphasizes that warm glow refers to the positive emotions arising from engaging in pro-environmental behavior. Warm glow also differs from positive feelings people experience in relation to non-environmental behaviors, such as leisure activities, because warm glow specifically arises when one's behavior aligns with one's personal values. In practice, however, definitions and operationalizations used in research do not always distinguish warm glow from closely related emotion constructs. A review of how warm glow has been defined and operationalized is therefore needed.

A unique feature of warm glow is its potential to perpetuate pro-environmental behaviors. This positive feedback loop between warm glow and pro-environmental behaviors may be self-reinforcing (Brosch, 2021; Brosch & Steg, 2021; Schneider & van der Linden, 2023; see Figure 1 for our conceptual framework). The first link in the loop is imagining how one would feel after engaging in a certain behavior. Such anticipated warm glow appears to drive pro-environmental intentions and behaviors. When expecting to feel good from pro-environmental behaviors, individuals report stronger intentions and also act more proenvironmentally in longitudinal studies (Jia & van der Linden, 2020; Strömbäck et al., 2025; van der Linden, 2018). In addition to self-reported behaviors, people with more anticipated warm glow also behave more pro-environmentally on incentivized behavioral tasks (Zhou, Brick, et al., 2026).

The second link in the feedback loop concerns people's feelings after they have engaged in pro-environmental behavior. Engaging in pro-environmental behaviors can generate positive feelings about oneself (Taufik et al., 2015; Zhou, Brick, et al., 2026). Individuals experience such good feelings because acting pro-environmentally signals to themselves that they are a good person (Venhoeven et al., 2016) whose actions contribute to the valued goal of protecting the environment. An individual who does not hold pro-environmental values would consequently not be expected to experience these benefits from the behavior.

The third link is that people who experience warm glow might anticipate more warm glow for similar future behaviors. Previous studies have found a strong positive association between anticipated and experienced warm glow (Zhou, Bosshard, et al., 2026; Zhou, Brick, et al., 2026). However, relatively few studies have investigated both feelings. Most findings suggest that experienced warm glow may be associated with pro-environmental behaviors (Bissing-Olson et al., 2016; Chatelain et al., 2018). This could potentially be due to a link through anticipated warm glow, as proposed in the positive feedback loop.

In recent years, there has been growing interest in examining associations between warm glow and pro-environmental behaviors and intentions. Research investigating this link is emerging in domains including psychology (Zhou, Brick, et al., 2026), economics (Antonetti & Maklan, 2014; Ma & Burton, 2016), and marketing (Adil, 2022; Chae et al., 2024). There is, however, no meta-analysis to date that directly examines warm glow as a distinct emotional construct related to pro-environmental behaviors. One meta-analysis of 12 effect sizes examined experienced warm glow as part of wellbeing (Zawadzki et al., 2020), while another meta-analysis focused on pride and pro-environmental behaviors (Shipley & van Riper, 2022). These findings provide valuable insights regarding positive emotions and proenvironmental behaviors, but they do not provide a synthesis of the entire body of evidence on warm glow. A systematic review and meta-analysis is needed to integrate research from different fields into a more comprehensive assessment of the link between warm glow and pro-environmental behaviors.

Intentions vs. Behaviors as Outcomes

Intentions are often a precursor of behaviors. However, individuals who show strong proenvironmental intentions may not always act accordingly. Thus, intentions are often viewed as a weak proxy of behaviors (Dablander et al., 2025; Sheeran & Webb, 2016). However, a substantial proportion of the existing literature of warm glow focuses on behavioral intentions rather than behaviors. Moreover, anticipated and experienced warm glow are strongly related to behavior intentions (Strömbäck et al., 2025), and intentions have been shown to mediate the relationship between anticipated warm glow and pro-environmental behaviors (Jia & van der Linden, 2020). Excluding intention-based research would consequently omit a considerable proportion of the available evidence. Thus, the present meta-analysis differentiates between pro-environmental intentions and behaviors while including both types of measures.

Moderators

In addition to estimating overall associations between anticipated and experienced warm glow with pro-environmental behaviors or intentions, we examined the conditions under which the strength of these relationships may be stronger or weaker. Understanding these conditions could inform the design of interventions that aim to leverage warm glow to promote pro-environmental behavior. Accordingly, we included several potential moderators in the meta-analysis.

One potential moderator is the domain of pro-environmental behavior. Environmentally relevant actions occur in many domains of life, such as consumption, travel, and civic engagement. These behaviors differ in terms of cost, effort, and environmental impact (Truelove & Gillis, 2018). Consequently, individuals may anticipate or experience more or less positive emotion across behaviors and behavior domains (Asutay et al., 2023; Strömbäck et al., 2025). For example, a person may expect to feel more positive towards sorting waste than towards eating less meat. Examining these differences can help identify domains in which warm glow may be especially impactful for motivating behaviors.

Methodological differences might also contribute to variation in findings. In particular, pro-environmental intentions and behaviors are often measured using different approaches, which may introduce variation across studies. For example, while self-reported measures are widely used in pro-environmental behavior research (Brick et al., 2024), they may lack validity in predicting real-life behaviors (Nielsen et al., 2022). In contrast, some studies use incentivized behavioral tasks to directly measure pro-environmental behavior (Zhou, Brick, et al., 2026). In this meta-analysis, we sought to examine whether the strength of the associations between warm glow and pro-environmental behavior differs systematically based on how behavior was measured.

Finally, a key question is how to sustain pro-environmental behaviors. External rewards can activate pro-environmental behaviors, but the effects usually do not persist in the long term (Dillman-Hasso, 2026). In contrast, intrinsic motivation, which might include rewarding feelings such as warm glow, are promising for encouraging sustained pro-environmental behaviors (Hartmann et al., 2017). A limited number of longitudinal studies suggest that people who anticipate or experience feeling good about pro-environmental behaviors take more action four weeks later (Jia & van der Linden, 2020; Zhou, Bosshard, et al., 2026). This leaves open the question of whether warm glow could promote pro-environmental behaviors recursively over time. To answer this question, we use the meta-analytic approach to systematically synthesize and compare the associations reported in different research designs (i.e., cross-sectional and longitudinal studies).

The Current Study

We present a pre-registered systematic review and meta-analysis to quantitatively examine associations between anticipated and experienced warm glow with proenvironmental intentions and behaviors, and to probe whether the strength of these associations differs across behavioral domains, measurement approaches, and research designs. We do not assess the relationship between anticipated and experienced warm glow because too few studies examined them both together. Additionally, we sought to provide an overview of how warm glow has been conceptualized to facilitate integration across this sprawling body of research. The conceptual framework and hypotheses are shown in Figure 1. Our main hypotheses were:

H1: Individuals who anticipate more warm glow will (H1a) report stronger proenvironmental intentions and (H1b) engage more in pro-environmental behaviors.

H2: Individuals who experience more warm glow will (H2a) report stronger proenvironmental intentions and (H2b) engage more in pro-environmental behaviors. Note. Dotted lines indicate the conceptual framework, and solid lines indicate the tested hypotheses. The testing framework is correlational because of the design of the available studies.

Methods

We conducted a systematic review and meta-analysis of empirical studies of warm glow and pro-environmental behaviors or intentions. Pre-registration, materials, analysis, and code are available online (https://osf.io/n8f5c/overview?view_only=e65a2d0919214e3fa896aae67591eff7). In the preregistration, we hypothesized correlational and causal relationships between warm glow and pro-environmental intentions and behaviors. However, there were not enough studies testing causal relationships to allow us to estimate those. Thus, we only tested the correlational hypotheses. The first author used ChatGPT (OpenAI, 2026) while preparing the manuscript to check grammar and expressions and to improve clarity and consistency. Example prompts included: "please let me know if there are any grammar and expression issues in this text"

and "please check the references and citations in this manuscript to see if there are any mismatches and if the references follow APA rules". In addition, after writing the original codes, the first author used Claude (Anthropic, 2026) to generate loop-based code to reduce repetitive code across the four meta-analytic models and to refine the code for generating figures. All AI-generated suggestions and code were reviewed and verified by the authors.

Eligibility Criteria

Papers were included based on six inclusion criteria: 1) published in English in peerreviewed outlets; 2) empirical studies; 3) quantitative measures of warm glow and proenvironmental behavior or intentions. We define warm glow as immediate, self-related positive feelings that people can experience from acting pro-environmentally, we thus only included studies where the measured emotions were specifically related to pro-environmental behavior or intentions. Studies measuring emotions towards climate change, for instance, were excluded; 4) more than half of the warm glow items needed to be about feelings rather than related constructs such as appraisals; 5) to avoid intervention effects, we included effect sizes only from control conditions with no intervention, or from studies in which participants freely chose to engage in pro-environmental behaviors. For example, we excluded studies in which participants were exposed to one of two messages about social norms (high social norm vs. low social norm) as the manipulation might influence the associations between warm glow and pro-environmental behaviors (or intentions); and last, 6) there was enough information for calculating effect sizes (i.e. zero-order correlation coefficients) from the information in the published article or as provided by the authors in response to our request (see Supplemental Section 4 for the email template we used). In addition, we deviated from the preregistration by excluding studies with daily diary designs. These designs generate a distinct data structure that is difficult to integrate with other studies.

Following the PRISMA procedure (Page et al., 2021) with additional suggestions from our academic librarian, we conducted our search for articles published up until February 9, 2026. The following databases were searched to identify eligible studies: Web of Science Core Collection, PsycINFO, Greenfile, and SocINDEX. These databases provide extensive coverage of psychology, social sciences, and sustainability science.

We included papers that contained both search strings: 1) pro-environmental behavior: environmental attitudes/ OR (((pro-environmental* OR proenvironmental OR green OR sustainab* OR climate-friendly OR climate friendly OR ecofriendly OR ecological OR environmental*) ADJ3 1 (behavio* OR act OR acting OR activit* OR donation* OR intention* OR attitud* OR concern* OR engagement* OR purchase*)) OR ((climate change OR climate policy OR climate action) AND (engagement OR action OR support OR strategy OR concern*)) OR (climate ADJ3 protection) OR conservation behavio*). 2) warm glow: positive emotions/ OR gratitude/ OR happiness*/ OR hope/ OR optimism/ OR pride/ OR well being/ OR altruism/ OR (altruis* OR feel* good OR feel* moved OR gratitude OR green glow OR happiness OR happy OR hope OR hopeful* OR joy OR optimis* OR positive affect* OR positive* emotion* OR pride OR proud OR satisfied OR triumph OR warm glow OR wellbeing OR well-being).

1 The operator "ADJ3" indicates that the two search terms appear within three words of each other in any order. Different databases have their own logic language and keywords settings. We list the complete search strings in Supplemental Section 1.

Selection Process

A total of 18,709 papers were identified. Duplicates were initially identified and removed using Zotero (Stillman et al., 2026). During the subsequent screening process, we used Rayyan (Ouzzani et al., 2016) to screen titles and abstracts, during which a small number of additional duplicate records were identified. In total, 5,373 records were removed as duplicates. The first author and one research assistant completed a screening evaluation. They screened the titles and abstracts using Rayyan. This resulted in 436 papers being included, of which nine lacked full text. For papers that were of doubtful fit, the full text was screened to establish whether to include them or not. Next, the first author, with two research assistants, started the stricter eligibility assessment and coding process by screening the full papers.

These three coders conducted pilot coding of three papers to ensure that they agreed on the process. After four rounds of pilot testing, the coders reached a high agreement rate of 88.3%. Identification of studies via databases Records screened (n = 13,336) Reports excluded (n = 348): Emotion towards others, not individual PEB/intention (n = 189) Non-empirical design (n = 43) Experiments which might influence the correlations (n = 32) No emotions (n = 22) Missing results (n = 16) More than half of the emotion measures did not measure emotion (n = 12) Dissertation (n = 11) No behaviors/intention (n = 10) Non-pro-environmental behavior (n = 7) Daily diary design (n = 2) Non-English (n = 2) Other (n = 2) Papers included in review (n = 92) Manually identified (n = 2) Identification Total included papers (n = 94) Total included effect sizes (k = 251) Screening Duplicate records removed before screening (n = 5,373) Included Records identified from: Web of Science (n = 14,324) PsycINFO (n = 2,153) GreenFile (n = 1,481) SocINDEX (n = 751) Reports sought for retrieval (n = 449) Records excluded (n = 12,900) Reports not retrieved (n = 9) Reports assessed for eligibility (n = 440)

Data Collection Process

We coded eight study features, which are displayed in Table 1. An eligibility assessment was also included, to detail the reasons for excluding certain papers. During the coding process, we found that some studies included measures of both anticipated and experienced warm glow. In such cases, the study was classified based on the framing represented by more than half of the measurement items. For unclear cases, the classification was determined through discussion among the authors. We also labeled the paper id and effect size id for later meta-analysis. We did not evaluate the quality of the studies. Most quality assessment tools evaluate the rationale of hypothesis generation and the appropriateness of data analysis methods, such as the JBI Critical Appraisal Checklist (Barker et al., 2023) and QATSDD (Sirriyeh et al., 2012). However, the relationships between warm glow and pro-environmental behaviors or intentions were often not the focus of the articles' hypotheses, and so a global quality assessment would not apply directly to our relationships of interest.

Effect Measures

Pearson's correlation coefficient (r) was used as the standard effect size metric to represent the correlations between warm glow and pro-environmental intentions or behaviors.

We converted other effect sizes, such as Spearman's rho correlations (Rupinski & Dunlap, 1996), into Pearson's correlation coefficients. We preserved point-biserial correlations as they are equal to Pearson's correlations. In addition, one study reported one-way ANOVA results, which we did not pre-register how to convert; we used the esc function (Lüdecke, 2018) in R to transform it into a Pearson's correlation coefficient. Correlations were not reported in 45 studies, among which five studies provided publicly available data. For these studies, we calculated Pearson's correlations in R. For the remaining studies, we contacted the authors to request the necessary data or correlation results. 24 authors replied with the requested information. However, some authors were unable to provide relevant information due to the original datasets being unavailable (e.g., loss of data storage), while others could not be reached despite repeated attempts. These studies were thus excluded for missing results.

Meta-analytic Approach

We followed the guidance from Harrer and colleagues (2021) on performing metaanalyses in R. Some effect sizes are nested within studies, such that there are several correlations of interest in one study with the same sample. These correlations are not independent. Thus, we used a three-level meta-analysis model to account for within-study variance (i.e., differences among multiple effect sizes from the same study), between-study variance, and variance from sampling errors (Konstantopoulos, 2011).

We tested our hypotheses separately for data from correlational and experimental studies.

For each model, we followed the same steps using the R package metafor (Viechtbauer, 2025). We first transformed Pearson's correlations into Fisher's z, as Pearson's r is usually not normally distributed. Fisher's z provides a more approximately normal sampling distribution for analysis. We conducted three-level meta-analysis models to calculate the pooled effect size with restricted maximum likelihood estimation. We used an adjusted weighted effect size which accounted for the three levels of variance to give effect sizes with higher precision (e.g., a smaller standard error) greater weight (Harrer et al., 2021). For ease of interpretation, we re-converted all effect sizes to Pearson's correlation coefficient in the results.

To assess total heterogeneity in the model, we used Cochran's Q, I² index, τ² and the prediction interval (Borenstein, 2024). Cochran's Q tested the presence of overall heterogeneity. A significant Cochran's Q test (p < .05) was taken as evidence that the observed variability in effect sizes exceeded that expected from sampling error alone, indicating the presence of overall heterogeneity. I² index further quantified the proportion of the total variance attributed to heterogeneity rather than sampling error. We calculated two I² indices: one reflecting the proportion of variance due to true effect size differences within studies, and another representing variance between studies. For between-study heterogeneity, we used the I² cut-offs of 25%, 50%, and 75% to indicate low, moderate, and large heterogeneity (Higgins et al., 2003). Regardless of the magnitude of heterogeneity, we interpreted the pooled effect size as the mean of a distribution of true effects. If moderate-tolarge heterogeneity (I² ≥ 50%) would be observed, we would emphasize the variability in effect sizes and the potential context-dependence of the effect (e.g., different domain of proenvironmental behaviors) rather than the generalizability of the pooled effects.

τ² indicated the absolute variance of true effects, with larger values indicating greater dispersion in true effects. If the confidence interval of τ² does not contain zero, it indicates that heterogeneity exists. The prediction interval provided a range within which the effect of a future study was expected to lie based on present evidence. A narrow prediction interval would suggest limited variation in true effects, whereas a wide interval would suggest substantial variation. If the prediction interval includes zero, the true effect in a new study could be null or opposite in sign to the pooled effect, even when the pooled effect is statistically significant.

We used the R package dmetar (Harrer et al., 2019) to calculate the level-specific I² statistics, whereas the other indices were obtained from models fitted using the metafor package (Viechtbauer, 2025). Each of these indices has strengths and limitations (Borenstein, 2024). Therefore, we used them together to evaluate the presence, proportion, magnitude, and implications of heterogeneity, and interpreted them jointly.

Sensitivity Analyses

We conducted sensitivity analyses to explain between-study heterogeneity (I² ≥ 50%) and to examine the robustness of the pooled effects. First, we identified influential cases using the leave-one-out method (i.e., recalculating the pooled effect after omitting each effect size in turn to see whether any single effect size changed the interpretation of results). Second, we used Baujat plots (Baujat et al., 2002) and formal influence diagnostics to identify influential cases. A Baujat plot provides a visual assessment of potentially influential cases. It shows the contribution of each study to the overall heterogeneity on the horizontal axis, and its influence on the pooled effect size on the vertical axis. Studies on the upper-right region of the plot were considered potentially influential as they contributed heavily to overall heterogeneity and had a relatively large influence on the pooled effect size. In addition, formal influence diagnostics, including standard residuals and Cook's distance, provide statistical measures for identifying influential cases. Studies were identified as influential when the absolute value of standard residuals exceeded the threshold of 3, or when its Cook's distance was above 4 divided by the total number of effect sizes (Viechtbauer & Cheung, 2010). We then conducted and reported the results of sensitivity analyses to evaluate the robustness of the pooled effect sizes when excluding these identified influential cases.

As mentioned, the included studies were different in many ways, and we therefore conducted moderator analyses to check whether the potential moderators would explain the heterogeneity. These moderators included domain and measurement approaches of proenvironmental behaviors or intentions, and research designs (i.e., cross-sectional vs.

longitudinal).

Our primary model included three levels to account for non-independence of effect sizes.

We also conducted two-level meta-analyses as a sensitivity analysis. Additionally, publication bias was assessed using funnel plots and Egger's regression tests. When publication bias was detected, we used multilevel PET-PEESE meta-regressions to adjust for small-study effects (Stanley & Doucouliagos, 2014). We did not use the trim and fill method (Duval & Tweedie, 2000), as previous simulation studies suggest that regression-based methods outperform it (Moreno et al., 2009). In addition, the PET-PEESE method is relatively straightforward to implement and interpret. Both PET and PEESE models are regressions based on a measure of precision. The PET model regresses observed effect sizes on standard errors and tests whether the intercept (i.e., the predicted effect size as the standard error approaches zero) is significantly different from zero. A significant intercept is taken as evidence that the underlying true effect is non-zero. The PEESE model is then applied to estimate the effect sizes after adjusting for small-study effect (Stanley & Doucouliagos, 2014).

Results

Study Characteristics

This meta-analysis included 251 effect sizes from 94 papers with a gender-balanced sample of 58,313 participants. Most studies were based in Asia, Europe, and the United States (see Figure 3). Overall, studies included anticipated and experienced warm glow, and there were more effect sizes on pro-environmental intentions (n = 172) than behaviors (n = 79;

Table 2). Note. Some studies included samples from multiple countries. Each country-specific sample was counted separately. Thus, the total number exceeds the number of included studies.

Definitions and Measurements of Warm Glow

30 studies provided a definition of warm glow (see Supplemental Table S1). Warm glow was generally defined as immediate, self-related positive feelings that people can experience from acting pro-environmentally when such actions align with their personal values.

However, the construct has been conceptualized in different ways across studies. Moral selfappraisal related to self-identity has been emphasized in some studies (e.g., feeling like a good or environmentally responsible person; Chen et al., 2025; Mahasuweerachai & Suttikun, 2022; Venhoeven et al., 2016), and feelings of satisfaction from pro-environmental behaviors in others (Rahnama Haratbar et al., 2024; Wang et al., 2023).

Different emotion items were used and combined to measure warm glow. Feelings of pride, feeling good, satisfaction, and happiness are the most frequently used items (Figure 4).

In some papers, there is no clear distinction between anticipated and experienced warm glow, since some studies use both anticipated and experienced framings in the measurement (Rahnama Haratbar et al., 2024; Torabi et al., 2025).

Meta Analysis

We conducted four separate three-level random effects models to analyze the pooled correlations for each of the following relationships: anticipated warm glow with proenvironmental intentions and behaviors, and experienced warm glow with pro-environmental intentions and behaviors. All hypotheses were supported: the pooled correlations for all four relationships were positive and significant based on 20 -43 studies with 26 -106 effect sizes. Individuals who anticipated more warm glow reported stronger pro-environmental intentions, r = .52, 95%CI [.47, .56], and engaged more in pro-environmental behaviors, r = .43, 95%CI [.35, .50]. Additionally, individuals who experienced more warm glow also reported stronger pro-environmental intentions, r = .53, 95%CI [.46, .59], and more proenvironmental behaviors, r = .45, 95%CI [.35, .55] (Table 2). Table 3 presents tests for heterogeneity across the four relationships. The Q statistic tests indicated significant heterogeneity. Most of the variance was attributable to between-study differences (I² : 68%-97%), with a smaller contribution from within-study differences (I² : 0%-29%), and negligible sampling error (I² : 2%-3%). The 95% confidence interval of τ² did not contain zero, and the prediction intervals were wide. Taken together, these results also indicated the presence of heterogeneity. In addition, the prediction interval for the relationship between experienced warm glow and pro-environmental behaviors contained zero, suggesting that some future studies might find a negative effect based on the current evidence.

Moderator Analyses

Domain of Pro-Environmental Behaviors and Intentions

Pro-environmental behaviors and intentions span multiple domains such as consumption, curtailment, civic engagement and nature conservation, and warm glow associations might vary across domains. Thus, we conducted a three-level meta-regression using domain as the moderator. Overall, no significant differences were found across domains (ps for four relationships: .11-.84). Figure 9 shows the pooled correlations by behaviors domains.

Furthermore, after accounting for the moderator, the Q statistic tests still indicated significant heterogeneity (ps < .001), indicating that substantial variability in effect sizes remained unexplained.

Measurement Approach of Pro-Environmental Intentions and Behaviors

Across the relationships between anticipated and experienced warm glow with intentions, self-report Likert scales were the most frequently used measure of intentions (k = 152). Selfreports with a binary answer scale were used less often (k = 16). Only four effect sizes were based on choice tasks measuring intentions. To measure behavior, self-reports were used most frequently, including frequency words (k = 43) and Likert-type scales (k = 23). Eight effect sizes were based on behavior measures involving incentivized tasks.

Meta-regression results using measurement approaches as a moderator suggested differing patterns across the four relationships. The association between anticipated warm glow and intentions was stronger when using self-report Likert scales compared to choice tasks, F(1, 104) = 6.62, p = .01. However, the numbers of effect sizes were unbalanced in the two conditions. The association between anticipated warm glow and behaviors was also moderated by the measurement approach, F(3, 49) = 4.32, p = .01. Results suggested that relationships based on self-report with strongly agree framings were significantly larger than the relationship based on the other three measurement approaches. The strength of associations between experienced warm glow and intentions and behaviors did not change across measurement approaches (intention: F(1, 64) = 1.94, p = .17, behavior: F(3, 22) = 1.53, p = .24). See Figures 10a and 10b for the pooled correlations by measurement approach.

Notably, based on the Q statistical tests, substantial heterogeneity remained after including measurement approach in the meta-analysis models (ps < .001).

Pooled Correlations by Measurement Approach

Research Design: Cross-Sectional vs. Longitudinal Studies

Longitudinal designs were rarely used to evaluate associations between warm glow and pro-environmental behaviors or intentions. Indeed, no longitudinal studies have examined the relationship between anticipated warm glow and intentions. Thus, we could not metaanalytically compare cross-sectional and longitudinal studies for the association between anticipated warm glow and intentions here. For the other three associations, we did conduct meta-regression analyses, as both cross-sectional and longitudinal designs were used.

The association between anticipated warm glow and pro-environmental behaviors was consistent between designs, F(1, 51) = 3.80, p = .06 (cross-sectional: r = .45, k = 33; longitudinal: r = .37, k = 20). In contrast, the association between experienced warm glow and pro-environmental intentions seemed to be influenced by design, F(1, 64) = 4.88, p = .03 (cross-sectional: r = .54, k = 65; longitudinal: r = .01, k = 1). However, there was only one effect size based on a longitudinal design. Finally, the association between experienced warm glow and behaviors was consistent between designs, F(1, 24) = 0.80, p = .38 (cross-sectional: r = .46, k = 22; longitudinal: r = .40, k = 4). Figure 11 shows the pooled correlations by design for three associations with longitudinal effects. Exploratory Analyses: Pride in Warm Glow Measurement

As shown in Figure 4, pride was the most frequently used item. However, pride is often studied as a separate emotion in relation to pro-environmental behaviors (e.g., Bissing-Olson et al., 2016; Onwezen et al., 2013; Rowe et al., 2019). It is unclear whether pride is more or less strongly associated with pro-environmental behaviors than other positive emotional experiences. We therefore conducted exploratory analyses to examine whether effect sizes differed between studies that did and did not measure pride.

Pride was commonly used, especially for anticipated warm glow. Pride only moderated the association between experienced warm glow and pro-environmental intentions. Studies that included pride showed stronger association than studies that did not include pride, F(1, 64) = 6.00, p = .02 (with pride: r = .41, k = 16; without pride: r = .56, k = 50). The other three relationships were consistent between pride measures. Figure 12 shows the pooled correlations by pride item across four relationships. In addition, the Q statistical tests still

Sensitivity Analyses

We conducted sensitivity analyses with the aim to explain the observed heterogeneity and to test the robustness of the pooled effects. First, leave-one-out analyses and analyses excluding studies based on standardized residuals and Cook's distance suggested no meaningful changes in the pooled effect sizes or heterogeneity with one exception. After leaving one effect size (Onwezen et al. (2014b)_1_2) out, the effect sizes of future studies might be negative as the prediction interval for the relationship between anticipated warm glow and behaviors contained zero, ranging from -.002 to .72 compared with original prediction interval ranging from .02 to .71. Second, regarding publication bias, visual inspection of funnel plots and Egger's tests provided evidence of small-study effects. Effect sizes were however robust after adjusting for publication bias. Additionally, two-level random effects model analyses revealed the same findings with no significant changes in the pooled effects and heterogeneity. Taken together, the pooled effects were robust to influential .46 .54 .38 .46 .56 .41 .39 .56 no yes, with pride item Pride Item Included number of effect si es 20 40 60 80 100 cases and to different analytic models.

Discussion

In this systematic review and meta-analysis, we synthesized evidence from 94 papers with 251 effect sizes on the relationship between warm glow and pro-environmental intentions and behaviors. Both anticipated and experienced warm glow had medium-to-large associations with pro-environmental intentions and behaviors (rs: .43 -.53). The results were robust after conducting sensitivity analyses. These findings provide strong evidence that warm glow is reliably positively associated with pro-environmental intentions and behaviors across behavioral domains, measurement approaches, and research designs. There was moderate variation in effect sizes, and this heterogeneity remained largely unexplained.

Below, we discuss the theoretical implications of these findings and consider several possible sources of the remaining heterogeneity, including differences in the conceptualization and measurements of warm glow, as well as methodological differences across studies. Finally, we note methodological limitations in the current literature and propose directions for future research.

A Promising Positive Feedback Loop

One prior meta-analysis has reported a positive association between experienced warm glow and pro-environmental behaviors across 12 effect sizes (Zawadzki et al., 2020). Our results, based on a larger body of work, are consistent with this finding. The present metaanalysis additionally suggests that anticipated warm glow shows similar patterns of association with both intentions and behaviors, which aligns with existing empirical studies that have included both (Jia & van der Linden, 2020; Strömbäck et al., 2025; van der Linden, 2018). Overall, this evidence suggests that warm glow may operate as both an antecedent and a consequence of pro-environmental behaviors (Schneider et al., 2021). These findings lend support to recent calls to consider emotions when trying to understand people's motivation to engage in pro-environmental behaviors (Becker & Veling, 2026).

One important feature of warm glow is the hypothesized positive feedback loop with behavior. For example, an individual may anticipate experiencing warm glow from choosing to travel by train rather than by plane, which could increase the likelihood of selecting the more sustainable option. After traveling by train, the individual may experience warm glow from acting in an environmentally friendly way. This positive emotion experience, in turn, might strengthen the expectation of experiencing warm glow from future pro-environmental behaviors, thereby reinforcing sustained pro-environmental engagements (Brosch, 2021; Brosch & Steg, 2021; Schneider & van der Linden, 2023). In this meta-analysis, we found strong and robust positive correlational evidence for several parts of this feedback loop: individuals who expect to feel warm glow also act more pro-environmentally and demonstrate strong behavioral intentions (Jia & van der Linden, 2020; Strömbäck et al., 2025; van der Linden, 2018). In addition, people experience warm glow following their proenvironmental behaviors and intentions (e.g., Taufik et al., 2015; Zhou, Brick, et al., 2026), likely because their behavior signals themselves as being a morally good person who has a positive impact on the environment (Venhoeven et al., 2016).

Our findings suggest that associations between warm glow and pro-environmental intentions and behaviors are robust across behavioral domains. Most studies on warm glow and pro-environmental behavior to date have focused on consumption and curtailment behaviors, which are commonly studied in the broader domain of environmental psychology research (Larson et al., 2015). Other types of actions, such as community engagement and organizational behaviors, are underrepresented in this literature. This imbalance may constrain the generalizability of current findings and underscores the need for research examining warm glow across a wider range of behavioral domains.

There is no obvious theoretical reason why the relationship between warm glow and proenvironmental behavior would vary across behavior domains. Within and across domains, pro-environmental behaviors do vary in costs, environmental impact and difficulty, however (Truelove & Gillis, 2018). It thus seems plausible that people might anticipate and experience different amounts of warm glow across different types of behaviors. Some research has suggested that anticipated warm glow is associated with low-but not high-cost proenvironmental behaviors, for instance (van der Linden, 2018). Previous research also suggests that individuals anticipate different amounts of warm glow from engaging in different behaviors (Strömbäck et al., 2025), based on the perceived impact of such behaviors (Asutay et al., 2023). Different features of behaviors, including costs, impacts and difficulty, may thus influence the relationship between warm glow and pro-environmental behavior.

Manipulating these features could clarify whether anticipated and experienced warm glow vary as a function of these characteristics. For example, the Work for Environmental Protection Task (Lange & Dewitte, 2021) allows for the costs and impacts of a given participant behavior to be manipulated. This could be used to test the extent to which warm glow is impact-driven vs cost-driven.

Finally, our results are also robust and consistent across intentions and behaviors, indicating that the positive associations with warm glow is not limited to pro-environmental intentions but also extends to behaviors. Moreover, while the approaches used to measure pro-environmental intentions and behaviors vary considerably, we also observed consistent findings across measurement approaches. In the studies included in our analysis, self-reports were most commonly used, consistent with research practices in environmental psychology more broadly (Brick et al., 2024). Our findings suggest that measurement approaches might only minimally affect the strength of the associations. For example, the association between anticipated warm glow and pro-environmental behaviors was stronger when behaviors were assessed using a self-report Likert scale (e.g., from strongly disagree to strongly agree) than using frequency words (e.g., never; often). One possible explanation is that different measurement approaches capture behavioral tendencies with varying levels of precision.

Importantly, relatively few studies have employed objective or quantitatively precise measures, such as behaviors measured in specific physical units, like energy or water consumption (e.g., Ramli et al., 2025). Given that self-reported measures are only weakly correlated with objective measures (Bosshard et al., 2024), using more objective measures could improve comparability across studies and facilitate the translation of behavioral outcomes into meaningful estimates of environmental impact (Nielsen et al., 2022).

Warm Glow in Research Practices

We observed considerable variability across the included studies in conceptualizations of warm glow. These differences are reflected in both measurement strategies and study designs.

Studies measured warm glow using different emotion terms, with some focusing on pride (e.g., Onwezen et al., 2013), and others assessing general positive feelings, such as satisfaction or feeling good (e.g., Ren et al., 2023). While measures like satisfaction might emphasize positive outcomes associated with environmental protection, pride may capture individuals' self-evaluations regarding their behavior efforts. Consistent with this distinction, several studies have specifically investigated the role of pride in pro-environmental behaviors (Bissing-Olson et al., 2016; Onwezen et al., 2013; Rowe et al., 2019) and previous metaanalytic evidence suggests that pride is strongly associated with self-reported proenvironmental behaviors and intentions (Shipley & van Riper, 2022). Preliminary results from our analyses suggest that pride and other positive emotions may slightly differ in their associations with pro-environmental behaviors. However, these analyses were exploratory, and it remains unclear whether the observed difference reflects a distinct role of pride or other differences between the studies. Further research directly comparing different positive emotions could help clarify whether specific emotions, such as pride, are more effective targets for interventions aimed at promoting pro-environmental intentions and behaviors.

When screening articles for potential inclusion, we noticed that some studies appear to blur the conceptual boundaries between warm glow and adjacent affective constructs. For example, some studies assess consumer or tourist satisfaction in environmentally relevant contexts, such as enjoyment of staying at a green hotel (Raza et al., 2023) or visiting an ecodestination (Chang et al., 2024). However, positive feelings in those contexts may arise from sources unrelated to the pro-environmental aspect of the behavior (e.g., service quality and comfort). We therefore did not include them in this review as they may not align with personal values, but it is possible that there is also evidence of warm glow in these contexts.

Another concern regarding the measurement of warm glow is the target of warm glow.

Most studies measured warm glow towards specific behaviors (e.g., recycling), while a few studies examined pro-environmental behaviors in general. Warm glow may vary across different pro-environmental behaviors (Strömbäck et al., 2025). This variability may be obscured by measures that assess warm glow toward pro-environmental behavior in general.

Similarly, some studies assessed warm glow separately for multiple behaviors and then aggregated the responses into a single indicator; aggregation may, however, mask meaningful differences in warm glow across behaviors. A behavior-specific target measure of warm glow could therefore provide a more precise measure of warm glow by reducing interpretation ambiguity for participants and allowing researchers to examine whether associations vary across behavioral domains.

Limitations and Future Directions

Substantial heterogeneity in the results remained unexplained after accounting for several moderators. This might be because of the diversity of included samples and designs. The populations are from many cultural contexts (see Figure 3), which have different values and norms about behaviors trying to protect the environment (Tam, 2025). Exploratory analyses with country as moderator yielded unstable results because of many country levels with very few effect sizes. Thus, we only report them as a descriptive overview in Supplemental Table S5. Moreover, the samples represent different populations, such as sustainable consumers and general citizens. Thus, diverse participant backgrounds might also contribute to the substantial heterogeneity of our findings.

Measurement timing may also explain the heterogeneity. For example, some studies assessed warm glow together with both past and future pro-environmental behaviors during a follow-up period. In such cases, two effect sizes were included when analyzing the pooled correlations: one capturing the association between warm glow and past behaviors, and the other capturing the association between warm glow and future behaviors. Because these effect sizes reflect different temporal relationships, including both in the analysis may have introduced ambiguity into the pooled estimates. While the present meta-analytic findings indicate a robust positive association between warm glow and pro-environmental intentions and behaviors, future research could systematically disentangle temporal ordering by explicitly distinguishing between past, current, and future behaviors.

Our findings provide strong correlational evidence consistent with the positive feedback loop between warm glow and pro-environmental behavior. However, causal evidence is still very limited: only two studies have explicitly manipulated warm glow feelings (Jerit et al., 2024; Lohmann et al., 2024). Thus, intervention and experimental studies were excluded from the present meta-analysis, and more experimental studies in this area are sorely needed.

To test whether anticipated warm glow causes pro-environmental behaviors would require anticipated warm glow to be manipulated. Given that warm glow is related to a target event, inductions of incidental emotions would not be suitable. Rather, methods like recalling past experiences of warm glow might be appropriate. A few studies have applied such methods to induce warm glow feelings and have found that they increase pro-environmental intentions (Jerit et al., 2024; Rowe et al., 2019). Experimental inductions of warm glow combined with objective behavioral measures would provide particularly strong causal evidence on whether warm glow leads to pro-environmental behaviors.

The second theorized link is from pro-environmental behavior to experienced warm glow. To test this causally, studies would need to manipulate behavior engagement to establish potential effects on the amount of warm glow people experience. However, it seems less likely that people would feel warm glow as a result of pro-environmental behavior that they did not choose to engage in. Therefore, manipulated behavior will be tricky to design, but important for testing the causal relationships between factors. Findings from well-being research suggest that engaging in pro-environmental behaviors, compared with engaging in one's usual daily activities, may increase well-being (Prinzing, 2024), potentially because of the warm glow people experience from acting pro-environmentally. Such designs gives participants the option to engage in pro-environmental behaviors or to continue with their usual activities. This could help experimentally vary behavioral engagement while preserving participants' sense of autonomy and allow for tests of the causal link between behavior and experienced warm glow.

Event-based daily diary designs are a complementary method to help capture the temporal relationships between warm glow and pro-environmental behaviors in real-life contexts. Daily diary designs have already been applied to test the relationship between incidental emotions and pro-environmental behaviors (Bissing-Olson et al., 2016; Doell et al., 2021). Such designs could be extended to warm glow. In addition, longitudinal research is warranted to test predictive links between warm glow and pro-environmental behavior in relation to longer-term wellbeing (Asutay et al., 2026).

Further work is also needed to probe for potential constraints to the potentially selfperpetuating loop between warm glow and pro-environmental behaviors. Warm glow feelings from previous pro-environmental actions may not motivate further engagement if the actor feels a sense of moral licensing, that is, perceiving their past morally good behaviors as permission to act in less environmentally friendly ways (Merritt et al., 2010). Moral licensing can reduce the motivation for subsequent pro-environmental action (Burger et al., 2022; Gholamzadehmir et al., 2019). Also, measures of other psychological factors such as social norms should be included as they might interact with warm glow to influence engagement in pro-environmental behaviors. For example, descriptive social norms could moderate the relationship between experienced pride and subsequent pro-environmental behaviors.

Specifically, people who experience greater pride are more likely to engage in proenvironmental behaviors when they perceive positive pro-environmental norms than when they perceive negative norms (Bissing-Olson et al., 2016).

One limitation of the present analysis is that we did not conduct a formal quality assessment or sensitivity analyses of study quality. This decision reflects broader methodological challenges in evaluating correlational evidence. Existing appraisal tools for correlational evidence, such as the JBI Critical Appraisal Checklist (Barker et al., 2023) and QATSDD (Sirriyeh et al., 2012), evaluate aspects of the overall study, including the clarity of hypotheses, appropriateness of methodology, and adequacy of statistical analyses. However, in many of the articles that were included in the current meta-analysis, the association between warm glow and pro-environmental intentions and behaviors was not the primary focus of the studies and was not necessarily specified in the hypotheses or examined in the main analyses. Thus, a high-quality study-level rating would not indicate that the association of interest was theoretically motivated, adequately hypothesized, or appropriately analyzed.

For this reason, appraising the quality of the study would not adequately capture the quality or interpretability of the specific effect sizes synthesized in the present meta-analysis. As an alternative indicator, we coded whether studies adopted open science practices, such as preregistration or open data sharing. However, only seven studies reported engaging in open science, which reflects the recent and gradual adoption of these practices. Consequently, these indicators do not seem to provide a good index of study quality that would allow for meaningful moderator analyses. Nevertheless, we hope that the increasing adoption of transparent research practices will strengthen future evidence synthesis efforts by improving reproducibility and reducing the risk of selective reporting.

Conclusion

Warm glow is gaining interest across disciplines because of its potential to stimulate a self-reinforcing feedback loop to motivate and sustain pro-environmental behaviors. In this pre-registered meta-analysis, evidence based on correlation findings suggests a robust and positive link between anticipated and experienced warm glow with both pro-environmental intentions and behaviors. Experimental and intervention studies are warranted to test the causal model of the feedback loop.

3.1 Outlier and Influential Studies

3.1.1 Leave-one-out Method

We re-analyzed the pooled effect sizes for each relationship by excluding one effect size each time in the model. Results suggested that the pooled correlations remained consistent across all iterations, with no substantial changes in heterogeneity or model variance.

Specifically, the association between anticipated warm glow and pro-environmental intentions ranged from .51 to .52, and association with behaviors ranged from .41 to .44. The pooled correlations between experienced warm glow and intentions and behaviors ranged from .51 to .54. Overall, these findings suggest that the results were robust and not unduly influenced by any single effect size.

3.1.2 Influence Diagnostics

Based on standard residuals, we only identified one effect size as an influential case (Zhao (2023)_1_1) for the relationship between experienced warm glow and proenvironmental intentions. The pooled correlation was robust after excluding this influential case (r: .51, original r: .53).

Using Cook's distance, we identified several influential effect sizes for the associations between anticipated warm glow and pro-environmental intentions and behaviors, and experienced warm glow and pro-environmental intentions. Regarding the association between experienced warm glow and pro-environmental behaviors, no studies were identified as influential cases. Excluding these influential effect sizes in the analysis decreased the between-study heterogeneity; the overall pooled effect sizes did not change meaningfully (Table 2). In addition, the Baujat plots showed a pattern of potentially influential cases that was consistent with the findings from the formal influence diagnostics (see Figure 1).

3.3 Two-level Model Analytic Results

To account for the interdependence of effect sizes in our meta-analysis, we used threelevel models to analyze the pooled effect sizes. In general, three-level models indicated a better fit to our data compared with two-level models, with a lower AIC and BIC, and significant results from the likelihood-ratio tests (Table 4). Here, we also report the results from standard two-level random effects models as a sensitivity analysis. Overall, the twolevel models also suggest moderate to large correlations between our variables of interest.

2. Definition of Warm Glow

Table S1 Definition of Warm Glow in Included Studies

The concept "warm glow" has been found to be an important approach for explaining contributions to public goods. In his model of impure altruism, Andreoni (1989 Andreoni ( , 1990) ) describes the motivation for voluntary contributions to a public good as "some private goods benefit from their gift per se" but does not provide a thorough explanation of the psychological processes behind this warm glow feeling. 3.2 Publication Bias

Funnel plots (Figure 2) and Egger's tests (Table 3) were used to assess small-study effects for all relationships. Egger's test uses standard variance as the predictor and effect size as the outcome. It showed significant results for all relationships (ps < .001), indicating that studies with larger standard errors (i.e. smaller sample sizes) tended to report large effect sizes. PET-PEESE methods were used to adjust for the small-study effect. As the intercept of four PET models were significant, it indicated that the true underlying effects were significantly different from zero. PEESE-models were then applied to provide a more reliable estimate of the effect sizes. The results were robust after using PEESE models to adjust for small-study effects (Table 3; rs: .41 -.58).

We did not use Cohen's kappa to assess inter-coder reliability because the small number of papers coded in each round could result in an unstable estimate with this method(Halpin, 2024). The two research assistants helped assess and code around 40 papers. After that, the first author completed the rest. During the coding process of the remaining articles, the first author discussed any uncertainties with the co-authors. Once all of the articles had been coded, the first author reviewed all of the papers again to ensure consistency. After the full text screening, 92 papers were retained. Finally, we added two recent papers that met the inclusion criteria but were not yet in the database. The final selection contained 94 papers with 251 effect sizes.
